57.title: The youngest son
57.hook: passing over his elder sons, Guru Ram Das names his youngest, Arjan, as the fifth Guru
57.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as the fifth Guru, chosen by his father, Guru Ram Das; the story of his choosing is told as another sign that the Guruship went to the one most devoted, not the one first in line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lavan, four rounds around the scripture. Your line was four rounds, one life. Which promise did you keep on purpose? Day fifty-seven.

At a family dinner there's the one who talks first, and the one who mostly listens. Guru Ram Das and Bibi Bhani had three sons. The eldest, Prithi Chand, was capable and ambitious, and he managed a lot of the practical business of the growing community. Tradition says he fully expected to be the next Guru. The middle son, Mahadev, was gentle and withdrawn, and seemed to want nothing to do with worldly affairs. And the youngest was Arjan. Quiet, devoted, still a young man. Today, the choice.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TALKS FIRST.` → `PRITHI CHAND, MAHADEV, ARJAN.` → `THE YOUNGEST, STILL A YOUNG MAN.`

segments.voice: Guru Ram Das chose Arjan. Tradition dates it to 1581, when Arjan was about eighteen. It made Prithi Chand bitterly angry. We'll hear more about that in a couple of days. Why Arjan? Sikh tradition tells of a test. The Guru needed someone to go to Lahore, to represent the family at a relative's wedding, and to stay there until he was called back. Prithi Chand found a reason not to go; he didn't want to be far away while the succession was being decided. Mahadev wasn't interested. Arjan simply went, and he waited, far from home, for a very long time. What happened while he waited is tomorrow's story. For today, look at the pattern. It has come up on this path before. Guru Nanak passed over his own sons for Lehna, the man who carried the wet grass. Guru Angad chose the old water carrier. Guru Amar Das chose the orphan with the tray of grams. And now Guru Ram Das passes over the confident eldest son for the quiet youngest one. Each time, the one who was ready wasn't the one who pushed forward. It was the one who served, and waited, and didn't make the moment about himself. One more thing changes here. From now on, the Guruship stays in Guru Ram Das's family. But the rule doesn't change: not the eldest, not the loudest, but the one who is ready. And with Guru Ram Das's choice, his part of the story closes: the orphan, the pool, the four rounds, the youngest son.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice someone quietly ready. Settle, and think. In your family, your office, your team, your friends. Who's the one who doesn't talk much in meetings, but always gets it done? Who's been waiting patiently for a chance nobody's given them? Bring their face to mind. Think about what they'd do if someone trusted them with more. The bell holds the time.
The youngest son. Arjan, chosen by Guru Ram Das over his elder brothers, to become the fifth Guru. Today's word.
Your line: the quiet one was ready. Today, give the quiet person in the room the first word, or the next job. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: Letters from Lahore
58.hook: sent away as a young man, Arjan writes longing letters to his father in verse (Majh, ang 96)
58.howItsDone: The Shabad Hazare, Guru Arjan's four verses of longing from Lahore, are in the Guru Granth Sahib in raga Majh, and some Sikhs include them in their morning prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the youngest son, chosen to be the fifth Guru. Your line was the quiet one was ready. Who did you give the first word to? Day fifty-eight.

Have you ever been far from someone you love, and written them a message you didn't send? Or sent it, and waited, and waited, and heard nothing back? Every few minutes, checking. Nothing. Yesterday we left young Arjan in Lahore. His father had sent him there and told him to stay until he was called. So he stayed. Weeks went by. Months. No word came. He missed his father, who was also his teacher, his Guru. So he wrote a letter. Not in prose. In verse. Today, the letters from Lahore.
screen: `A MESSAGE, AND NO REPLY.` → `ARJAN WAITS IN LAHORE.` → `HE WRITES TO HIS FATHER, IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: The letter was a short hymn, and it's in the scripture, in raga Majh. Its first line says, in paraphrase: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru. It cries out like the rainbird, the chatrik, which in Indian poetry waits and calls for the one raindrop it will drink. My thirst isn't quenched, the verse says, and I can't find peace without the sight of my beloved. He sent it. No reply. He wrote a second verse, even more aching. It says, in paraphrase, that it has been so long since he saw his beloved's face. Still nothing. Here's what tradition says was happening. His eldest brother, Prithi Chand, was intercepting the letters. He didn't want Arjan anywhere near their father while the succession was open. So when Arjan wrote a third, which says that a single moment apart feels like the dark age, he marked it with a number: three. That letter reached Guru Ram Das. The Guru saw the three, asked about the first two, and found out what had happened. He sent for Arjan at once. When they met again, Arjan sang a fourth verse, the joy of reunion, and together the four make one hymn. Sikhs call it the Shabad Hazare, and some include it in their morning prayers. Two things stand out. First, longing isn't treated as weakness here. The Gurus' hymns use the language of missing someone for the soul missing God, and in this hymn, missing a father and missing God are sung as one ache. Second, tradition tells the waiting as the test. Arjan never stopped writing, and he never stopped waiting.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line to someone you miss. Find a pen, or open a note on your phone. Think of someone you miss: far away, out of touch, or gone. Don't write a whole letter. One line. What you'd say if they were in the room. Take the whole time to find the right words, then write them down. Whether you send it is up to you. The bell holds the time.
Letters from Lahore. Young Arjan's verses of longing to his father, intercepted twice, and now a hymn in the scripture. Today's word.
Your line: my mind longs. Today, if you miss someone, don't hide it; send them the line you wrote, or call. Day fifty-eight.

59.title: A jealous brother
59.hook: his elder brother Prithi Chand resents him and makes trouble for years
59.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Prithi Chand's rivalry as a hard chapter in Guru Arjan's life, and read Guru Arjan's hymns of protection and trust in God, some sung in daily prayers, with those years in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, letters from Lahore, and a third letter with a number on it. Your line was my mind longs. Did you send the line to someone you miss? Day fifty-nine.

Who got the bigger room. Who Dad liked more. Some arguments outlive the house they started in, and a holiday dinner turns into careful choices about where people sit. The Bible tells stories like this too: Cain and Abel, Joseph and his brothers. The Sikh story has one. Arjan was now the fifth Guru. And his eldest brother, Prithi Chand, the one who had intercepted the letters, did not accept it. Tradition says he never did. Today, the jealous brother, and what Guru Arjan did about him.
screen: `WHO DAD LIKED MORE.` → `CAIN AND ABEL, JOSEPH'S BROTHERS.` → `PRITHI CHAND DOES NOT ACCEPT IT.`

segments.voice: Prithi Chand set himself up as a rival Guru. Tradition says he gathered his own followers, collected offerings that were meant for the Guru's kitchen, so that for a while the langar at Amritsar ran short, and even wrote hymns of his own and signed them with the name Nanak, as if they were the Gurus' words. Bhai Gurdas, the Sikh poet, gave his followers a sharp name: minas, the deceivers. And tradition tells darker stories too, of attempts to harm Guru Arjan's young son, Hargobind: a nurse with poison, a snake, a poisoned dish. Each time, the stories say, the child was spared. How did Guru Arjan respond? That's the heart of this day. He didn't raise an army against his brother. He didn't curse him. He kept doing his work: building, singing, serving the community. And he trusted his son's life to God. In the scripture there are hymns of Guru Arjan's full of gratitude for protection. In one, he says, in paraphrase, that the hot wind cannot touch the one who is under God's shelter. Sikh tradition links some of them to those years. So today's line, pray for the difficult one, doesn't mean pretending it's fine. In the story the offerings really go missing and the child is really in danger. What the Guru refuses is to become like his brother: he leaves him to God and keeps his own work going. A Guru, and still a brother, across the table from someone who wanted his place.
screen: `A RIVAL GURU, A HUNGRY KITCHEN.` · `DARKER STORIES: THE CHILD SPARED.` · `NO ARMY, NO CURSE. HE KEPT WORKING.` · `THE HOT WIND CANNOT TOUCH HIM.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE DIFFICULT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a family tension, no fixing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one difficult relationship in your family, or close to it. Don't replay the argument. Don't plan what you'll say next time. Just let the person's face be there, and notice what happens in your chest. If you pray, you can hold them before God, whatever words you use. If you don't, just wish them one good thing. The bell holds the time.
A jealous brother. Prithi Chand, who resented Guru Arjan for years, and whom the Guru answered with work and trust, not revenge. Today's word.
Your line: pray for the difficult one. Today, when that person comes to mind, wish them well once, even if it's through your teeth. Day fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 59 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HOUSE WITH FOUR DOORS.`

60.title: The house with four doors
60.hook: Guru Arjan builds the Harmandir Sahib low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all
60.howItsDone: The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara for Sikhs; visitors of every faith cover their heads, walk down into the complex, circle the pool, and eat together in its langar, which serves people day and night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jealous brother, and a Guru who answered with work, not revenge. Your line was pray for the difficult one. Did you wish them well, even once? Day sixty.

Think about how important buildings are usually designed. They sit up high, on a hill or on a platform. There's a grand staircase going up. There's one main entrance, maybe with a guard. The meaning is clear: this place is above you, and you come in by permission, through the front. Now picture the pool at Amritsar, the one Guru Ram Das began. His son, Guru Arjan, finished it, and then he did something unexpected. In the middle of the water, he began to build a house of God. And almost every choice he made about that building turns the usual meaning upside down. Today, the house in the middle of the pool.
screen: `HIGH UP, ONE GRAND ENTRANCE.` → `THE POOL AT AMRITSAR.` → `A HOUSE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: It's called the Harmandir Sahib. Hari is a name for God, mandir means temple or house, and Sahib is a word of respect. The house of God. Many people know it as the Golden Temple, because of the gold that covers it; that came much later, in the nineteenth century. Here's what Guru Arjan did. First, instead of raising it high, he set it low. You walk down steps to reach it, so everyone who enters, rich or poor, comes down a little. Humility is built into the architecture. Second, instead of one grand entrance, he gave it doors on all four sides. In a world where people were sorted by caste and by creed, this house was open from every direction, to everyone. North, south, east, west. Remember Guru Nanak's feet toward the Kaaba, and the question: which way is God not? Here's that question turned into a building. And tradition adds one more detail. Many Sikhs say that the foundation stone was laid by a Muslim Sufi, Mian Mir, a friend of the Guru's from Lahore. Historians debate that story, but it has been told for a very long time, and it fits the house. The building was finished around 1604. It stands in the middle of the pool, reached by a causeway, and to this day the langar there feeds tens of thousands of people every day, of every faith and none. The house with four doors is still open on every side. What Guru Arjan placed at its center is the story of the next few days.
screen: `HARMANDIR — THE HOUSE OF GOD.` · `SET LOW: YOU WALK DOWN TO ENTER.` · `FOUR DOORS, FOR EVERY DIRECTION.` · `A FOUNDATION STONE, TRADITION SAYS.` · then, large: `OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door and leave it open. Settle first. Then, if you can, get up and open a door: your front door, a window, the door to your room. Stand in it for a moment. Feel the air come through. Think of who you'd welcome through it, and who you might have kept out without meaning to. Leave it open, for a while, if it's safe. The bell holds the time.
Harmandir Sahib. The house of God at Amritsar, set low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all. Today's word.
Your line: open on every side. Today, open one door you've kept shut: a conversation, an invitation, a seat at your table. Day sixty.

61.title: Gathering the hymns
61.hook: with Bhai Gurdas as scribe, he gathers the Gurus' hymns and those of other saints into one book
61.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Arjan as the compiler of the Adi Granth, the book that became the Guru Granth Sahib, and the hymns of Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Farid and other saints are sung in gurdwaras alongside the Gurus' own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir Sahib: built low, with a door on every side. Your line was open on every side. Did you leave a door open for someone? Day sixty-one.

A grandmother's lullaby. The hymn at every funeral. The tune someone hums in the kitchen. Songs like these often live only in people, and when the people go, verses slip away, words drift, and sometimes someone adds a verse of their own and passes it off as the old one. By the time of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the Sikh community had four Gurus' worth of hymns, sung every day, copied in handwritten books kept by different families. And tradition says others were starting to write hymns in Guru Nanak's name that he never wrote. Guru Arjan decided the words needed one home. Today, the gathering.
screen: `SONGS THAT LIVE IN PEOPLE.` → `FOUR GURUS' WORTH OF HYMNS.` → `ONE HOME FOR THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says that around 1603, at a quiet spot by a pool near Amritsar, Guru Arjan sat down to make a book. His scribe was Bhai Gurdas, a scholar and poet who was also the Guru's relative, and whose own verses Sikhs still read. The Guru dictated; Bhai Gurdas wrote. First, the Guru gathered. Earlier Gurus' hymns had been collected in handwritten volumes under the third Guru, and tradition says those books were kept by his son, Baba Mohan, who would not hand them over. So Guru Arjan went to his house and sang outside his window, a hymn in his honor, until Mohan came down and gave them up. Second, the Guru sorted. He set the hymns not by author or by date, but by raga, the musical mode each one was meant to be sung in, so the book is laid out like a songbook for the day and its moods. Third, and this is the surprise, he opened the book to others. Beside the Gurus' words he placed hymns by saints from outside the Sikh community: Kabir, a weaver from Benares; Namdev, a calico printer; Ravidas, a leatherworker whom his society called untouchable; and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi who had lived centuries before. Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, sitting on the same pages; Sikhs understand it as the Guru hearing in them the same truth about the one God. And he left some things out: the hymns written falsely in Nanak's name did not go in. Gather, sort, open the pages, and guard them. That is how a scattered songbook became one book.
screen: `GURU ARJAN DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.` · `SINGING FOR THE OLD BOOKS.` · `SORTED BY RAGA, LIKE A SONGBOOK.` · `KABIR, RAVIDAS, FARID ON ONE PAGE.` · then, large: `ONE HOME FOR THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather one thing worth keeping. Settle and breathe for a moment. Then let your mind go looking, the way the Guru went looking. A line someone said to you that you've never forgotten. A recipe only one person in your family knows. A song, a joke, a piece of advice. Pick one. Now picture where it lives right now: in one person's head, on a scrap of paper, in a phone that could break. Just hold it for a while, and ask where it would be safe. The bell holds the time.
Gathering the hymns. Guru Arjan, with Bhai Gurdas writing, collected the Gurus' hymns and those of other saints, sorted them by raga, and made them one book. Today's word.
Your line: gather what is true. Today, write down the thing you chose, or ask the person who holds it to tell you again, and keep it somewhere safe. Day sixty-one.

62.title: The Adi Granth installed, 1604
62.hook: the book is placed in the Harmandir and Baba Buddha reads the first hukam
62.howItsDone: Every day in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened and a hymn read at random as the hukam, the day's word; the hukam from the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is shared widely each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gathering the hymns: Guru Arjan and Bhai Gurdas made one book. Your line was gather what is true. What did you find worth keeping? Day sixty-two.

The book is finished. Page after page, written by hand, every hymn set under its raga. Now what? You could put it on a shelf. You could keep it in the Guru's own room. Guru Arjan did neither. In 1604 the book was carried in procession to the Harmandir Sahib, the house with four doors in the middle of the pool, from day sixty. Tradition says the old man Baba Buddha, who had known Guru Nanak as a boy, carried it on his head, and the Guru walked behind with a whisk, waving it over the book the way you'd honor a king. Today, the book gets a home.
screen: `THE BOOK IS FINISHED.` → `CARRIED ON BABA BUDDHA'S HEAD.` → `THE GURU WALKS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Adi Granth. Adi means first, or original. Granth means book. The first book. That's what Sikhs call this volume, the one Guru Arjan compiled. Much later, it would become the Guru Granth Sahib, and that's a story for another day. For now, watch what happens in the Harmandir. The book is placed on a raised seat in the center, under a canopy. And the Guru sits below it. Lower than the book. The man who made it takes a humbler place than the words. Baba Buddha is named as the first granthi, the keeper and reader of the book. And then comes a moment Sikhs still repeat each day. He opens the book at random, and reads the hymn at the top of the left page. That reading is called a hukam, an order, or a word for the day. Tradition says the very first hukam was a line of Guru Arjan's own saying, in plain words, that God himself stands up to carry out the work of the saints. A fitting word for a new house. That same practice goes on now, in gurdwaras all over the world. Every morning the book is opened, and a random hymn is read as the word for the day. Some Sikhs look up the Harmandir Sahib's hukam on their phones before breakfast. A practice from 1604, in your pocket. The words were gathered, sorted and guarded. Now they have a home, a keeper, and a voice.
screen: `ADI GRANTH — THE FIRST BOOK.` · `THE GURU SITS LOWER THAN THE BOOK.` · `BABA BUDDHA, THE FIRST READER.` · `A HUKAM, A WORD FOR THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE WORD HAS A HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open any book and read one line. Whatever's nearest: a novel, a cookbook, a book of poems, a holy book if you have one. Don't choose the page. Let it fall open. Read the first line your eye lands on, slowly, twice. Then close the book and sit with the line, the way a room full of people sits with the day's hukam. It may seem to mean nothing. It may land exactly. Just let it be the word you were handed. The bell holds the time.
Adi Granth. The first book, compiled by Guru Arjan and installed in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604, with the Guru seated below it.
Your line: the word has a home. Today, give one thing that matters to you a proper place: a shelf, a clean corner, a spot on the table. Day sixty-two.

63.title: Arrest at Lahore
63.hook: summoned by the emperor Jahangir's order, Guru Arjan is imprisoned and tortured in the heat of Lahore
63.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Arjan's imprisonment and torture in Lahore in the hymns, sermons and stories of his martyrdom anniversary each summer, and the site in Lahore is marked by Gurdwara Dera Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Adi Granth: carried into the Harmandir, with the Guru seated below it. Your line was the word has a home. Did something of yours get its proper place? Day sixty-three.

Look at the week behind you. A quiet youngest son chosen as Guru. Letters of longing from Lahore. A jealous brother. A house with four doors, a book gathered from many voices, and that book given a home. Guru Arjan has built a great deal in a short time, and people are noticing. Crowds come to Amritsar. The community is growing, organized, confident. And in 1605 a new emperor, Jahangir, takes the throne in the Mughal capital. Within a year, his order reaches the Guru. Come to Lahore. It is early summer on the plains of Punjab, the hottest time of the year. Today, the week that began in longing for Lahore ends there.
screen: `A WEEK OF BUILDING.` → `A NEW EMPEROR, JAHANGIR.` → `COME TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Why was the Guru arrested? The sources give more than one answer, and historians weigh them differently. Jahangir himself left a memoir, and in it he writes about the Guru with open irritation: too many people, Hindus and Muslims both, were following him, and the emperor wanted it stopped. There was also politics. Jahangir's own son, Prince Khusrau, had rebelled, and Jahangir's memoir itself says the prince stopped to see the Guru on his way; the Sikh accounts say the Guru blessed him, as he blessed anyone who came. And Sikh tradition adds a court official, Chandu Shah, who held a personal grudge. What the Sikh accounts agree on is what happened next. The Guru was held in Lahore, and in the heat of summer he was tortured. Tradition remembers it in terrible detail: made to sit on a red-hot iron plate, with burning sand poured over him. We won't linger on it. What Sikhs linger on is how he sat. A friend came: Mian Mir, a Muslim Sufi saint of Lahore, whom tradition remembers as close to the Guru. He was horrified, and offered to go to the emperor and plead for him. Tradition says the Guru calmly told him not to, that this too was within God's will, and that he would bear it. In the Sikh accounts, he did not shout. He did not curse the emperor. He sat, and stayed steady, and kept remembering. That word from day seven, simran, is doing its hardest work here. Tomorrow, how it ended, and what Sikhs call him because of it.
screen: `WHY? MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.` · `HELD IN THE HEAT OF LAHORE.` · `MIAN MIR OFFERS TO PLEAD.` · `STEADY, AND REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `STEADY IN THE HEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in stillness for one minute, and then a little longer. Nothing to fix. Nothing to answer. Let your body get still first, hands in your lap, feet on the floor. Notice anything that wants you to move: an itch, a thought, a sound. Don't fight it and don't follow it. Stay. If you remember a name for God, you can let it ride on your breath. If not, just let the breath be your anchor. The bell holds the time.
Arrest at Lahore. In 1606, on the emperor Jahangir's order, Guru Arjan was held and tortured in the summer heat, and stayed steady.
Your line: steady in the heat. Today, when something gets heated, a message, a meeting, a traffic jam, take one still breath before you answer. Day sixty-three, the end of another week.
